outputs.text: What did you do today, and how did you feel about it? Share a few highlights or small moments, and I’ll turn them into a short, personal blog post.

I'd be glad to write it, but I don't know anything about your day yet. I can't see your calendar either: Google Calendar needs to be authorized in your claude.ai connector settings first.

Could you send me a few quick notes? For example:

What you did, from morning to evening
Anything that stood out, like a win, a surprise, a frustration or a conversation
Who the post is for, such as a personal blog, a company or team blog, or friends
The tone you want: reflective, funny, casual or professional
A rough length, like 150, 300 or 500 words

Rough bullet points are fine. Once I have them, I'll write the post in plain text with no markdown, headings or emoji.

Spent today thinking about how much work an agent actually takes off your plate. It does the task, sure. But if I'm sitting there watching it, then checking everything again, how much did I really delegate? I wanna hand something over and go get lunch. That's the bar.

And then there's selling. We're confident about the product, but people aren't gonna magically hear about it because we spent another day making it better. You have to actually get it in front of them. Sounds obvious when I say it like that. Somehow there's always one more thing to fix first.

Anyway, that's where my head was today. Make it good enough that people trust it with their work. Get someone to try it. See where they get nervous. Probably plenty to do tomorrow too.

I don't know what actually happened today, so I built this draft from things you've said: the hike, the agent you're building, selling, and the fundraise. Swap in the real details.

Today was one of those days where nothing big happened but it felt like a lot.

Morning I went hiking with the team. Not the slow scenic kind. Who the hell wants to go like that? Head down, hit the top, grab a makgeolli, come back. Honestly the best meetings we have happen on the way down. Someone says something half-tired and it turns out to be the thing we've been missing for two weeks.

That's actually the whole reason we're building what we're building. Those conversations are so useful but it's so awkward to pull out your phone and start recording. Nobody does it. So the stuff just disappears. I wanna get an agent to just catch it.

Afternoon was sales. My guy next to me kept texting me that we're basically doing volunteer work right now, and he's not wrong. We're confident about the product, like actually confident. But confidence doesn't pay anybody. The hard part is getting the brand out there and selling until it can survive on its own. So I spent most of the afternoon on calls trying to get people to pay us for something they already say they love.

Had a quick call with an angel in the evening too. Nice person. But I keep coming back to the same thing. If we're going for a big valuation, like a fucking huge valuation, then another 100k here or there doesn't really move anything. What moves it is people using it and paying for it. So that's what I'm thinking about going to bed.

Good day. Tired legs. Still haven't sold enough. Tomorrow again.

Wednesday in Taipei started with a short call with a mentor, mostly scheduling follow-ups. I told my agent to send the message as is.

Around 4pm, someone opened my Arca Ring web card on an iPhone and left nothing. I had trimmed the demo an hour earlier, so a tap shows only the web card. Later, an attendee at the hackathon opened it and tapped through to LinkedIn. A third tap came in the evening, and again nothing was left. Three taps in one day is a start.

I got to the c0mpiled-18 venue on Nanjing East Road at 17:35. It's the YC Startup School Hackathon. The power failed for a while during orientation, and there are 15 judges, some here and some in the US. The clock started at 18:00, and submission is at 22:45.

At 20:00 I started building with parallel agents: one for my own voice data, one for training, one for the web demo, one for the paper. The idea is an AI that writes like a specific human, trained on his real context.

First ring tap today in Taipei. Someone opened the Arca Ring web card and left nothing.

I'd trimmed the demo an hour earlier. Just the web card now. No App Clip overlay. Less stuff between the tap and the person.

By the third tap, at the hackathon, another attendee opened the card. Nothing left again.

I want the interaction to take almost nothing. Then I look at the nothing and try to figure out what it means. Very reasonable founder behavior.

Privacy should include the right to open something and disappear. No little receipt for me saying whether it made sense. I think that's right. Still want the receipt, apparently.

An interface can get out of someone's way so completely that I can't tell whether it worked or they just left.

The card opened. That much I know.

I'd like to know more. That's the awkward part.
What happened over your last few days? Share a few details about what you did, who you spent time with, and how you felt, and I’ll turn them into a 300-word essay.

I can't write this yet because I don't know anything about your last few days. I tried to search your Gmail for recent messages, but that permission wasn't granted. Google Calendar and Google Drive aren't connected either; you can authorize them in your claude.ai connector settings. The folder I'm working in only holds temporary tool files, so there's nothing about your days there.

You have two options:

1. Give me a few rough notes about what happened, how you felt about it, and anything that stood out. Fragments are fine. I'll turn them into a 300-word essay in plain text, with no markdown, headings or emoji.

2. Approve Gmail access and ask again. I'll piece your days together from your recent email. Keep in mind that email shows your work and errands better than how things actually felt, so a sentence or two from you would still make the essay better.

The last few days, I keep coming back to the same thing. We can make something useful. Okay. But can we get someone to actually hand over the work and feel good about it?

Because those are pretty different things. Someone tries it, says it's cool, and then goes back to doing everything themselves. What did we accomplish there? We gave them a demo. That's basically it.

I think what I want is pretty simple. You're having a conversation, something useful comes up, and you don't have to stop being in the conversation to save it. Or you've got something to do, you give it to an agent, and you can actually leave. Go grab a drink. Think about something else. If you're watching the whole time, checking every little thing, you might as well do it yourself.

But then there's the selling part. I keep thinking about the product because that's the part I want to think about. There's always something to fix. And usually it really does need fixing, so it's pretty easy to justify another day of that.

Meanwhile, we still have to explain why someone should pay us. In a way they understand immediately. That's hard. You can spend so much time inside something that you forget which part sounds useful to anyone outside it.

Same with fundraising. A huge number is exciting, sure. But tomorrow morning you're still there, trying to get the thing to work and trying to get people to use it.

So that's where my head's been these last few days. I feel confident, then impatient, then I find another thing we should probably fix. I want to move faster. I also want to be able to hand someone the product without giving them a whole speech first.

Here. Try it. That's the goal.

I tried to check your Gmail for what actually happened, but the permission was denied. So this essay is built from the one note I found locally (agents, delegation, selling) and the lines you gave me. It doesn't make up any specific meetings or events. Send me a few real moments and I'll rewrite it around them.

Last few days I kept coming back to one question. How much work does an agent actually take off your plate? It does the task, sure. But if I'm sitting there watching it, then checking everything again after, how much did I really delegate? Basically nothing. I just moved the work around. I wanna hand something over and go grab lunch. That's the bar. The metric we're watching pretty closely right now is how much success you feel when you delegate. Not how smart the thing is in a demo. How it feels when you walk away.

The other thing in my head was selling. We're honestly confident about the product. But nobody's gonna magically hear about it because we spent another day making it better. You have to actually put it in front of people. Sounds obvious when I say it like that. Somehow there's always one more thing to fix first, and then another week is gone. My guy next to me keeps saying we can't sell like this, and he's right. Right now we're basically doing volunteer work.

The hard part isn't building. The hard part is getting the brand out there and selling until it can survive on its own. Our target is people with taste. They archive everything, they notice what's off, and they're the ones who'll tell their friends. So we don't need everybody. We need the right people to try it and see where they get nervous.

So that's the plan going into this week. Make it good enough that people trust it with real work. Get someone to try it. Watch where they hesitate, fix that, and do it again. Head down, hit the halfway point, then maybe grab a makgeolli. Plenty to do tomorrow too.

Four days, three cities, one idea that kept changing shape.

On Saturday I was in Korea, up past one in the morning researching competing recording rings: what they cost, how long the battery lasts, who makes them. I found a smart-ring OEM and asked what a single sample would cost. An hour later I plugged in an ESP32 and told my agent to put Arca's face on that tiny screen, so it could live inside a 3D-printed device. In the evening I spent an hour on a call with the ring maker. They won't share source, but they offer an SDK, an API and BLE support. I told them I wanted a sample first, so I could check the app connection and Bluetooth myself.

Sunday was fellowship orientation in Seoul. I pitched Arca as a personal agent that remembers who you met, when, and what was said, with a ring to swap contacts instead of business cards. I admitted I want to be Korea's first twenty-something trillionaire. That night I slept at the office.

Monday was hackathon day. I built Tender, an API reverse-auction router, and watched a teammate's 3D simulator wow the room. Then I packed for a morning flight to Taipei.

On Tuesday, late at night, the demo check passed: tap the ring and the note lands on my phone in about eight seconds.

Today the ring went out into the world. The first tap came from a stranger who opened the web card and left nothing. Another attendee tapped through to LinkedIn. Honestly, the quiet taps taught me as much as the engaged ones.

By evening I was at the c0mpiled-18 hackathon in Taipei. The power failed for a while, which felt right for a hackathon. At eight I started building with parallel agents: one for my own voice data, one for training, one for the web demo, one for the paper. The idea is an AI that writes like a specific human, trained on his real context. Tonight, that human is me.

Saturday night in Korea, I was looking up recording rings. Battery life, who makes them, whether I could get a sample. My question was pretty basic. Can I make one that looks high quality with this?

Then I plugged in an ESP32 and asked the agent to put Arca's face on the tiny screen. I wanted it to live inside a 3D-printed device. Apparently an agent needs a face now. I'm the one giving it housing.

There is always another thing to check. The Bluetooth connection. The app. Whether the thing in the picture can actually become something you wear. I wanted a sample so I could check it myself. Hard to stay abstract when something has to fit on a finger.

On Sunday, at a founders fellowship in Seoul, I pitched Arca as a personal agent that remembers who you met, when, and what you said. A ring to swap contacts instead of business cards.

A room full of people meeting each other, and my pitch was a better way to keep track of meeting each other. I think that's useful. I also think remembering what someone said and being there when they say it are two separate jobs. I can build for one. The other still has to be me.

I told friends I'd probably sleep at the office that night.

By Wednesday in Taipei, people were opening the ring's web card. The first person left nothing. At the hackathon, an attendee tapped through to LinkedIn. Another opened the card and left nothing.

Three taps. One LinkedIn click. That's what I can account for.

It's tempting to make the next question about the card. What should appear first. What would make someone leave their details.

But what do I remember about the person who left nothing?
